# Grupo Frontera Political Controversy

## 1. Background and Formation

### 1.1 Grupo Frontera Overview

Grupo Frontera is an American regional Mexican music band formed in 2022 in Edinburg, Texas . The band consists of six members: Adelaido "Payo" Solís III (lead vocals and bajo quinto), Juan Javier Cantú (second vocals and accordion), Alberto "Beto" Acosta (congas), Carlos Guerrero (drums), Brian Ortega (bass), and Carlos Zamora (accordion) . Although the majority of the members were born in the United States, they maintain strong cultural ties to Mexico, with their ancestors originating from Tamaulipas and Nuevo León .

The band's musical style is characterized as norteño, a traditional Mexican regional genre that has experienced a significant resurgence in popularity in recent years . What distinguishes Grupo Frontera from other norteño bands is their ability to blend traditional musical elements with contemporary influences, creating a sound that appeals to both older and younger audiences . Their fashion style also reflects this fusion, as they typically wear modern streetwear brands like Prada or Balenciaga, contrasting with traditional norteño attire .

### 1.2 Musical Career and Rise to Fame

Grupo Frontera's breakthrough came in 2022 with their cumbia version of the Colombian band Morat's song "No Se Va" . This cover went viral on TikTok, eventually charting on the Billboard Hot 100 at number 57 and becoming the fifth regional Mexican song to appear on this prestigious chart . The band's success continued with subsequent releases, including collaborations with major artists such as Bad Bunny on "Un x100to," Fuerza Regida on "Bebé, dame," and Peso Pluma on "Tulum" .

In 2023, the band released their debut album "El Comienzo" (The Beginning), which featured several hit songs and collaborations . The album's success was recognized at the 25th Annual Latin Grammy Awards, where "El Comienzo" won the award for Best Norteño Album, while the single "El Amor de Su Vida" won Best Regional Mexican Song . This marked a significant achievement for the young band, which had only been together for about a year at the time of these prestigious awards.

Their rapid rise to fame was further evidenced by their inclusion in major music festivals and events. In 2023, they performed at the celebration of Mexico's Independence Day in the Zócalo of Mexico City, an event headed by then-President Andrés Manuel López Obrador . They were also scheduled to perform at the 2025 Sueños Music Festival in Chicago, alongside artists such as Shakira and Don Omar .

### 1.3 Political Neutrality Prior to 2025

Before the controversy erupted in early 2025, Grupo Frontera had maintained a notably apolitical stance throughout their career. In an interview with EL PAÍS published on January 5, 2025, band member Juan Javier Cantú explicitly stated: "We rarely get involved in politics. It's very controversial for us and we just want to make music" . This sentiment was echoed by other members of the band, who consistently emphasized their focus on their musical career rather than political matters.

The band's apolitical stance was also reflected in their charitable activities. In the same EL PAÍS interview, Cantú and Alberto "Beto" Acosta highlighted their donation of toys to children at a community center for deported immigrants affected by border policies . When asked about the U.S.-Mexico border wall, Acosta shared the band's disagreement with the concept, while Julián Peña Jr. commented on its incomplete status . These statements indicated a general concern for immigrant communities without explicitly endorsing any particular political party or candidate.

Their previous interactions with political figures had been largely ceremonial and non-partisan. For instance, they had performed at events organized by both Democratic and Republican officials in Texas, including the declaration of February 16, 2023, as "Grupo Frontera Day" in Edinburg, Texas . Such appearances were viewed as cultural celebrations rather than political endorsements, reinforcing their image as musicians who sought to unite rather than divide through their music.

## 2. The Political Controversy

### 2.1 The Viral Video and Initial Accusations

The political controversy surrounding Grupo Frontera began in late January 2025 following the viral spread of a TikTok video . The video showed the grandmother of band member Adelaido "Payo" Solís III, known as "La Abuela Frontera," dancing to the song "YMCA" by Village People after voting . This video immediately sparked controversy because "YMCA" had become closely associated with Donald Trump's 2024 presidential campaign .

The controversy was exacerbated when social media users claimed that the band had deleted several videos from their social media accounts that allegedly showed band members expressing support for Trump . A TikTok user identified as @sarahjasmine\_\_ alleged that she had seen videos of Grupo Frontera members stating they would vote for Trump, but that these videos had been removed . She claimed: "There's a video where you can see Grupo Frontera saying they vote for Trump. Now that they're canceling different Latino influencers who support Donald, I have to talk about this because I saw them" .

The situation escalated when users discovered what they believed to be additional evidence of political support. They claimed to have found screenshots of the band members' personal Instagram accounts following Trump's profile and liking his posts . Furthermore, some users alleged that the band had deleted a TikTok video in which they themselves were dancing to the same "YMCA" song as Solís's grandmother .

### 2.2 Social Media Backlash and Boycott Calls

The accusations against Grupo Frontera triggered an immediate and severe backlash on social media platforms, particularly on X (formerly Twitter) and Instagram . The band's social media accounts, which had accumulated over 2.3 million followers, were flooded with negative comments and criticism . Many fans expressed feelings of betrayal, arguing that the band was turning its back on its own community by supporting policies that negatively affected Mexican immigrants .

The backlash was particularly intense among Mexican fans, who viewed any association with Trump as a betrayal given his well-known anti-immigration stance and policies . Social media users began calling for a boycott of the band, using hashtags such as #CancelGrupoFrontera and accusing the band of being "traitors" to the Latino community . Messages on social media included statements like: "Make music, not politics" and "We don't want racists here" .

The controversy also led to a significant drop in the band's social media following. Reports indicated that they lost thousands of followers in a short period of time . The negative sentiment extended beyond mere unfollowing, with many fans expressing their intention to stop listening to the band's music entirely and urging others to do the same .

### 2.3 The [Change.org](https://Change.org) Petition

The social media backlash culminated in the creation of a [Change.org](https://Change.org) petition on February 11, 2025, calling for Grupo Frontera's removal from the 2025 Sueños Music Festival lineup . The petition, created by an individual using the alias "Espíritu," argued that the band's alleged support for Trump was incompatible with the festival's celebration of Latin music and culture .

The petition stated: "We want this because Grupo Frontera has been caught and found out to be Trump Supporters. This does not sit well with Latinos who may or may not be fans of the group but will not support racism. We Latinos stand united in boycotting Grupo Frontera and if they are not removed from the line-up, we will go as far as Boycotting Sueños Music Festival as well. La Raza Unida... Jamas sera Vencida!" 

The petition gained significant traction, accumulating over 9,700 signatures by February 12, 2025 . The festival's co-founder, Christopher Den Uijl, responded to the controversy by posting on Instagram that the festival supports the Latino community and that none of the co-founders support the president, though he did not specifically mention Grupo Frontera . Despite the controversy, Grupo Frontera remained on the festival lineup, and the event took place as scheduled on May 24-25, 2025 .

## 3. Grupo Frontera's Response

### 3.1 First Official Statement (February 7, 2025)

After several weeks of silence amid the growing controversy, Grupo Frontera released their first official statement on February 7, 2025, through their Instagram Stories . The statement was brief but direct, in which the band categorically denied any political affiliation or alliance with any party that opposes immigrants and the Latino community .

In this initial statement, the band emphasized their own immigrant backgrounds, stating that they and their families are immigrants from the border region . They also reaffirmed their support for the Mexican people and clarified that "the opinions of our friends and family do not represent the band" . This statement was seen by many as an attempt to distance themselves from the political controversy while acknowledging their community ties.

The band's statement came after days of mounting pressure from fans and social media users demanding clarification on their political stance. Prior to this official response, the band had maintained radio silence on the matter, with their social media accounts continuing to post content unrelated to the controversy, including a video collaboration with Spanish artist Alejandro Sanz .

### 3.2 Second Statement and Video Response (February 22, 2025)

On February 22, 2025, Grupo Frontera released a more detailed video response on Instagram, seeking to address the controversy more comprehensively . In this video, lead vocalist Adelaido "Payo" Solís III made several key statements aimed at 澄清 the band's position and refuting the accusations.

Solís began by stating: "We are migrants, our parents are migrants, and we tell you straight up, we do not support any political party that is against migrants" . He went on to address the misinformation that had spread on social media, saying: "On TikTok there have been so many false news stories that we are constantly having to deny each one... we can't keep up... The only opinions that matter in Grupo Frontera are those of the members, no one else can speak for us" .

The video also included explanations for some of the controversial content that had surfaced. Regarding the deleted TikTok video of the band dancing to "YMCA," the band claimed it was simply a backstage routine from their previous tour, the "Jugando a Que No Pasa Nada Tour," where they had danced to songs from their elementary school years . They denied that this was in any way related to political support for Trump.

Alberto "Beto" Acosta also addressed the band's initial silence, explaining that they had been overwhelmed by the amount of "fake news" circulating on the internet and had not known how to respond . He emphasized that the band's primary focus remained on making music and supporting their community, stating: "We are migrants, we are for migrants... and to the fans, you know what we have done, you know what we have supported for our race, whether in Mexico, the United States, or wherever we are, and that is what Grupo Frontera represents" .

### 3.3 Media Interviews and Additional Clarifications

In addition to their social media statements, Grupo Frontera gave several interviews to media outlets in an attempt to further clarify their position. One of the most significant was their interview with EL PAÍS, conducted in Madrid on January 5, 2025, and published shortly before the controversy erupted . In this interview, which took place before the viral video emerged, the band members had already expressed their general stance on politics and immigration.

During the interview, when asked about Trump's re-election and his proposals regarding the border with Mexico, Juan Javier Cantú responded: "We rarely get involved in politics. It's very controversial for us and we just want to make music. But we've always supported immigrants. Last year, we went to visit a \[community] center: we donated toys for the children. It's our neighborhood, after all" .

Alberto "Beto" Acosta added: "We respect the laws that the country has, but we support immigrants as best we can. We do things for the community. We donate toys for the children of the migrants who are there and who are being detained \[by the authorities]" . When specifically asked about their stance on the border wall, Acosta stated that the band disagreed with the concept, while Julián Peña Jr. noted that it was only half-built .

The band also gave an interview to Jesse Cervantes for EXA FM, where they affirmed their commitment to the immigrant community and their pride in Mexican culture "without distinction of ideologies or borders" . In the red carpet interview at the 37th Lo Nuestro Awards, when asked about the controversy by Cuban-American television host Raúl de Molina, the band appeared visibly uncomfortable. Peña's response—"We dedicate ourselves to music. We love everyone and want peace and love. Take care of yourselves"—was criticized by fans as inadequate and evasive .

## 4. Reactions and Consequences

### 4.1 Public and Media Reception

The public reception of Grupo Frontera's statements was overwhelmingly negative, with many fans and social media users viewing them as insincere attempts to protect the band's reputation rather than genuine expressions of their beliefs . Critics pointed out that the band had not explicitly denounced Trump by name, which they saw as a significant omission .

The media coverage of the controversy was extensive, with major outlets on both sides of the border covering the story. Mexican media outlets such as Infobae, TV Azteca, and Milenio provided detailed coverage of the controversy, often taking critical stances toward the band . American media outlets including the Chicago Sun-Times, Latin Times, and The Direct also covered the story, with some focusing on the broader implications for Latino artists in the United States .

Some media outlets attempted to provide more balanced coverage. The Chicago Sun-Times noted that the connection between the band and Trump might simply be a matter of shared musical taste, suggesting that both might enjoy "YMCA" by Village People without any political significance . However, this perspective was largely overshadowed by more critical coverage that emphasized the potential betrayal of the Latino community.

The controversy also sparked broader discussions about the role of Latino artists in American society and the expectations placed upon them to represent community values. Some commentators argued that artists should be free to hold their own political opinions, while others maintained that given their platform and influence, Latino artists have a responsibility to align their public positions with the best interests of their community .

### 4.2 Impact on the Band's Career

The political controversy had a significant impact on Grupo Frontera's career, both in terms of their public image and their professional opportunities. The band experienced a substantial drop in social media followers, with reports indicating they lost thousands of followers in the weeks following the controversy . Their social media platforms continued to receive 大量 negative comments, with many users expressing their intention to stop supporting the band .

Despite the controversy, the band's scheduled performances continued as planned. They performed at the 2025 Sueños Music Festival in Chicago on May 25, 2025, alongside artists such as Shakira and Don Omar . However, there were reports of protests at some of their concerts, and videos emerged showing alleged booing during their performances, though some of these were later revealed to be manipulated or taken out of context .

The controversy also affected the band's relationships with other artists. Several prominent Latino artists spoke out against the band, including Ángela Aguilar, who had previously collaborated with them on the song "Frágil" . Other artists who had been vocal about their opposition to Trump's policies, such as Residente, Selena Gomez, and Lupillo Rivera, were praised by fans for their stance, while those who remained silent, including Grupo Frontera initially, faced criticism .

The band's commercial success also appeared to be affected by the controversy. While specific sales figures were not widely reported, industry analysts noted a decline in the band's chart performance and streaming numbers following the controversy . The band had been scheduled to perform at several high-profile events in Mexico, but there were reports that some of these bookings were canceled or postponed due to the controversy .

### 4.3 The Aguilar Family Conflict

The Grupo Frontera controversy also sparked a public feud within the Aguilar family, one of Mexico's most prominent musical families. The conflict began when Emiliano Aguilar, son of legendary Mexican singer Pepe Aguilar, released a song titled "Ilegal" in February 2025, which was a direct criticism of Trump's deportation policies .

In the song, Emiliano Aguilar raps: "Todos somos habitantes del mundo y en nuestra tierra nadie debería ser ilegal" (We are all inhabitants of the world and on our earth no one should be illegal) . The song was accompanied by the hashtag #TheWallIsNotEnough and was described by the artist as "a hymn for migrant workers who face the siege of American authorities" .

Following the release of "Ilegal," Emiliano Aguilar took to Instagram to express his anger toward Grupo Frontera, posting a series of stories with strong language, including "Fuck Grupo Frontera. Mexico deserves respect" . His brother Leonardo Aguilar, however, expressed support for the band in the comments section of one of their posts, writing: "Don't worry. The fans will continue supporting you. The others are people with nothing to do. We know who you are" .

This led to a public argument between the brothers, with Emiliano responding with more inflammatory posts, including one where he referred to Leonardo as "gallito fino" (fancy rooster) and accused him of indifference toward the immigrant community . Emiliano wrote: "Here's a Mexican who dies for his race with his balls in the right place... You've always had everything, you've never lacked the attention and love of the public" .

The conflict between the Aguilar brothers added another layer of controversy to the already tense situation. According to Jessica Luna of TVNotas, Emiliano later deleted his posts after reportedly receiving a reprimand from their father, Pepe Aguilar . However, the public feud had already drawn significant attention and further highlighted the deep divisions within the Latino community regarding political allegiances and cultural identity.

## 5. Analysis and Assessment

### 5.1 Media Coverage Analysis

The media coverage of the Grupo Frontera political controversy revealed significant biases and varying approaches to reporting on the issue. Mexican media outlets generally took a more critical stance toward the band, often framing the controversy as a betrayal of the Mexican and Latino communities . These outlets frequently emphasized the band's Mexican roots and the contradiction between their cultural identity and their alleged political sympathies.

Infobae, one of the leading Mexican news outlets, published multiple articles on the controversy, including pieces with headlines such as "Grupo Frontera reacciona a críticas por presunto apoyo a Donald Trump y rechazo a migrantes" (Grupo Frontera reacts to criticism for alleged support for Donald Trump and rejection of migrants) . The coverage often included emotional language and emphasized the negative impact on the band's fanbase, particularly among Mexican fans who felt betrayed.

American media coverage was more varied in its approach. Some outlets, such as The Direct, provided factual reporting of the controversy without taking a clear stance, focusing on the timeline of events and the various statements from the band and their critics . Other outlets, such as Latin Times, framed the controversy within the broader context of Latino celebrities and their political responsibilities, noting that while many artists had spoken out against Trump's policies, Grupo Frontera had remained silent for weeks .

The Chicago Sun-Times took a more nuanced approach, suggesting that the connection between the band and Trump might be overblown. The paper noted that both the band and Trump might simply share a taste in music, rather than political beliefs . However, this perspective was in the minority, with most media coverage emphasizing the political implications of the controversy.

Social media played a crucial role in amplifying the controversy, with platforms like X and TikTok serving as primary sources of information for many people. The viral nature of the original video and the subsequent backlash demonstrated the power of social media in shaping public opinion and influencing the trajectory of such controversies .

### 5.2 Notability of the Controversy

The Grupo Frontera political controversy meets multiple criteria for notability in the context of Wikipedia standards. The controversy received extensive coverage in reliable sources, including major news outlets such as EL PAÍS, Infobae, Latin Times, and the Chicago Sun-Times . The coverage was sustained over several months, from the initial viral video in late January 2025 through the band's responses in February and the ongoing discussions throughout the year.

The controversy also had significant cultural and social impact. It sparked debates about the role of Latino artists in American society, the expectations placed on cultural figures, and the relationship between personal political beliefs and public responsibility . The controversy even led to a public feud within the prominent Aguilar family, demonstrating its reach beyond the band itself .

The controversy's impact on the band's career, including lost followers, canceled performances, and damaged reputation, further demonstrates its notability . The fact that the band was scheduled to perform at major events such as the Sueños Music Festival and faced public protests and petitions for their removal indicates the controversy's significance within the music industry and Latino community .

Additionally, the controversy occurred within a broader context of political tensions in the United States, particularly regarding immigration policies under the Trump administration. This context gave the controversy added significance, as it represented a microcosm of larger societal divisions .

### 5.3 Long-term Implications

The Grupo Frontera political controversy has had lasting implications for the band, the Latino music industry, and discussions about political responsibility in entertainment. For the band specifically, the controversy marked a turning point in their career trajectory. Prior to the controversy, they had been experiencing rapid success, winning Latin Grammy awards and collaborating with major artists . The controversy, however, damaged their reputation among a significant portion of their fanbase, particularly in Mexico and among politically active Latino communities in the United States.

The controversy also highlighted broader issues within the Latino music industry regarding political neutrality and public responsibility. Artists like Ángela Aguilar, who had collaborated with Grupo Frontera on the song "Frágil," faced questions about whether they should sever ties with the band . The situation created a precedent where artists' political beliefs, or even perceived beliefs, could significantly impact their professional relationships and opportunities.

The controversy also had implications for the broader discussion about Latino identity and political affiliation. It highlighted the tensions between cultural identity and political ideology, particularly for Mexican-American artists who straddle both cultures . The band's statement that they are "migrants supporting migrants" while maintaining American citizenship reflected these complex identities .

From a social perspective, the controversy revealed deep divisions within the Latino community regarding political allegiance and the role of public figures. The intense backlash against the band demonstrated the high expectations placed on Latino artists to represent community values, particularly regarding immigration issues . The fact that some fans defended the band's right to hold their own political opinions, while others called for their cancellation, showed the complexity of these discussions .

The controversy also had implications for the music industry's approach to artist management and crisis communication. The band's initial silence and delayed response were widely criticized, suggesting that artists need more sophisticated strategies for handling political controversies . The speed at which misinformation spread on social media platforms also highlighted the challenges of managing public perception in the digital age.

Looking forward, the Grupo Frontera controversy will likely serve as a case study for other Latino artists navigating political controversies. It demonstrates the potential consequences of political neutrality in polarized times and the importance of clear, timely communication when addressing sensitive issues. The controversy also underscores the need for artists to consider the broader implications of their actions and statements, particularly when they have significant influence within their communities.

## 6. Conclusion

The Grupo Frontera political controversy of 2025 represents a significant moment in the intersection of music, politics, and cultural identity. What began as a viral video of a band member's grandmother dancing to a popular song evolved into a full-blown controversy that challenged the band's relationship with their fanbase, their industry peers, and the broader Latino community.

The controversy emerged against a backdrop of heightened political tensions in the United States, particularly regarding immigration policies under the Trump administration. The band's alleged association with Trump, based primarily on circumstantial evidence and social media speculation, triggered intense backlash from fans who viewed such support as a betrayal of their Mexican heritage and immigrant community values.

Grupo Frontera's response to the controversy was characterized by initial silence followed by carefully worded statements that attempted to clarify their position while avoiding explicit political endorsements. Their statements emphasized their own immigrant backgrounds and support for migrant communities, but these efforts were largely unsuccessful in appeasing their critics, who viewed the statements as insufficient and potentially disingenuous.

The controversy's impact extended beyond the band itself, sparking debates about the political responsibilities of Latino artists and the tensions between personal beliefs and cultural representation. The public feud within the Aguilar family further highlighted these tensions, demonstrating how political controversies can divide even those within the same cultural and professional circles.

From a journalistic perspective, the controversy revealed both the power and the limitations of social media in shaping public opinion and the challenges of reporting on complex issues involving cultural identity and political affiliation. The speed at which misinformation spread and the difficulty in verifying certain claims highlighted the challenges of maintaining accuracy in the digital age.

The Grupo Frontera controversy ultimately serves as a reminder of the complex relationship between artists and their communities, particularly in politically polarized times. It demonstrates how seemingly small events can snowball into major controversies when they touch on sensitive issues of identity, loyalty, and political belief. The controversy also underscores the importance of clear communication and thoughtful consideration of public responsibility for artists who wield significant influence within their communities.

As the dust settles on this controversy, its long-term impact on Grupo Frontera's career and the broader Latino music industry remains to be seen. However, it has already established itself as a significant event that will likely be referenced in discussions about political controversy in Latin music for years to come. The controversy's lessons about the intersection of music, politics, and culture will continue to resonate as Latino artists navigate an increasingly complex and politically charged landscape.

The Grupo Frontera political controversy thus stands as a notable example of how modern media, social platforms, and political polarization can transform a minor incident into a major cultural moment, with lasting implications for all parties involved.

Grupo Frontera's statement came after days of mounting pressure from fans and social media users demanding clarification on their political stance.

Prior to this official response, Grupo Frontera had maintained radio silence on the matter, with their social media accounts continuing to post content unrelated to the controversy, including a video collaboration with Spanish artist Alejandro Sanz.
On February 22, 2025, Grupo Frontera released a more detailed video response on Instagram, seeking to address the controversy more comprehensively.
In this video, Grupo Frontera lead vocalist Adelaido "Payo" Solís III made several key statements aimed at clarifying the band's position and refuting the accusations.
Adelaido "Payo" Solís III began by stating: "We are migrants, our parents are migrants, and we tell you straight up, we do not support any political party that is against migrants".

Adelaido "Payo" Solís III went on to address the misinformation that had spread on social media, saying: "On TikTok there have been so many false news stories that we are constantly having to deny each one... we can't keep up... The only opinions that matter in Grupo Frontera are those of the members, no one else can speak for us".
The video also included explanations for some of the controversial content that had surfaced regarding Grupo Frontera.

Regarding the deleted TikTok video of Grupo Frontera dancing to "YMCA," the band claimed it was simply a backstage routine from their previous tour, the "Jugando a Que No Pasa Nada Tour," where they had danced to songs from their elementary school years.
Grupo Frontera denied that this was in any way related to political support for Trump.

Alberto "Beto" Acosta also addressed Grupo Frontera's initial silence, explaining that they had been overwhelmed by the amount of "fake news" circulating on the internet and had not known how to respond.

Alberto "Beto" Acosta emphasized that Grupo Frontera's primary focus remained on making music and supporting their community, stating: "We are migrants, we are for migrants... and to the fans, you know what we have done, you know what we have supported for our race, whether in Mexico, the United States, or wherever we are, and that is what Grupo Frontera represents".
In addition to their social media statements, Grupo Frontera gave several interviews to media outlets in an attempt to further clarify their position.
One of the most significant interviews was with EL PAÍS, conducted in Madrid on January 5, 2025, and published shortly before the controversy erupted.
During the EL PAÍS interview, which took place before the viral video emerged, the band members had already expressed their general stance on politics and immigration.

During the interview, when asked about Trump's re-election and his proposals regarding the border with Mexico, Juan Javier Cantú responded: "We rarely get involved in politics. It's very controversial for us and we just want to make music. But we've always supported immigrants. Last year, we went to visit a [community] center: we donated toys for the children. It's our neighborhood, after all".

Alberto "Beto" Acosta added: "We respect the laws that the country has, but we support immigrants as best we can. We do things for the community. We donate toys for the children of the migrants who are there and who are being detained [by the authorities]".
When specifically asked about their stance on the border wall, Alberto "Beto" Acosta stated that Grupo Frontera disagreed with the concept, while Julián Peña Jr. noted that it was only half-built.

Grupo Frontera also gave an interview to Jesse Cervantes for EXA FM, where they affirmed their commitment to the immigrant community and their pride in Mexican culture "without distinction of ideologies or borders".
In the red carpet interview at the 37th Lo Nuestro Awards, when asked about the controversy by Cuban-American television host Raúl de Molina, Grupo Frontera appeared visibly uncomfortable.
Julián Peña Jr.'s response—"We dedicate ourselves to music. We love everyone and want peace and love. Take care of yourselves"—was criticized by fans as inadequate and evasive.

The public reception of Grupo Frontera's statements was overwhelmingly negative, with many fans and social media users viewing them as insincere attempts to protect the band's reputation rather than genuine expressions of their beliefs.
Critics pointed out that Grupo Frontera had not explicitly denounced Trump by name, which they saw as a significant omission.
The media coverage of the controversy was extensive, with major outlets on both sides of the border covering the story.
Mexican media outlets such as Infobae, TV Azteca, and Milenio provided detailed coverage of the controversy, often taking critical stances toward Grupo Frontera.
American media outlets including the Chicago Sun-Times, Latin Times, and The Direct also covered the story, with some focusing on the broader implications for Latino artists in the United States.

The Chicago Sun-Times noted that the connection between Grupo Frontera and Trump might simply be a matter of shared musical taste, suggesting that both might enjoy "YMCA" by Village People without any political significance.
This perspective was largely overshadowed by more critical coverage that emphasized the potential betrayal of the Latino community.
The controversy also sparked broader discussions about the role of Latino artists in American society and the expectations placed upon them to represent community values.

Some commentators argued that artists should be free to hold their own political opinions, while others maintained that given their platform and influence, Latino artists have a responsibility to align their public positions with the best interests of their community.
The political controversy had a significant impact on Grupo Frontera's career, both in terms of their public image and their professional opportunities.
Grupo Frontera experienced a substantial drop in social media followers, with reports indicating they lost thousands of followers in the weeks following the controversy.
Grupo Frontera's social media platforms continued to receive a large amount of negative comments, with many users expressing their intention to stop supporting the band.
Despite the controversy, Grupo Frontera's scheduled performances continued as planned.
Grupo Frontera performed at the 2025 Sueños Music Festival in Chicago on May 25, 2025, alongside artists such as Shakira and Don Omar.

There were reports of protests at some of Grupo Frontera's concerts, and videos emerged showing alleged booing during their performances, though some of these were later revealed to be manipulated or taken out of context.
The controversy also affected Grupo Frontera's relationships with other artists.
Several prominent Latino artists spoke out against Grupo Frontera, including Ángela Aguilar, who had previously collaborated with them on the song "Frágil".

Other artists who had been vocal about their opposition to Trump's policies, such as Residente, Selena Gomez, and Lupillo Rivera, were praised by fans for their stance, while those who remained silent, including Grupo Frontera initially, faced criticism.
Grupo Frontera's commercial success also appeared to be affected by the controversy.
While specific sales figures were not widely reported, industry analysts noted a decline in Grupo Frontera's chart performance and streaming numbers following the controversy.
Grupo Frontera had been scheduled to perform at several high-profile events in Mexico, but there were reports that some of these bookings were canceled or postponed due to the controversy.
The Grupo Frontera controversy also sparked a public feud within the Aguilar family, one of Mexico's most prominent musical families.
The conflict began when Emiliano Aguilar, son of legendary Mexican singer Pepe Aguilar, released a song titled "Ilegal" in February 2025, which was a direct criticism of Trump's deportation policies.
In the song, Emiliano Aguilar raps: "Todos somos habitantes del mundo y en nuestra tierra nadie debería ser ilegal" (We are all inhabitants of the world and on our earth no one should be illegal).
The song was accompanied by the hashtag #TheWallIsNotEnough and was described by the artist as "a hymn for migrant workers who face the siege of American authorities".

Following the release of "Ilegal," Emiliano Aguilar took to Instagram to express his anger toward Grupo Frontera, posting a series of stories with strong language, including "Fuck Grupo Frontera. Mexico deserves respect".

His brother Leonardo Aguilar, however, expressed support for Grupo Frontera in the comments section of one of their posts, writing: "Don't worry. The fans will continue supporting you. The others are people with nothing to do. We know who you are".

This led to a public argument between the brothers, with Emiliano responding with more inflammatory posts, including one where he referred to Leonardo as "gallito fino" (fancy rooster) and accused him of indifference toward the immigrant community.
Emiliano Aguilar wrote: "Here's a Mexican who dies for his race with his balls in the right place... You've always had everything, you've never lacked the attention and love of the public".
The conflict between the Aguilar brothers added another layer of controversy to the already tense situation.
According to Jessica Luna of TVNotas, Emiliano Aguilar later deleted his posts after reportedly receiving a reprimand from their father, Pepe Aguilar.
However, the public feud had already drawn significant attention and further highlighted the deep divisions within the Latino community regarding political allegiances and cultural identity.
The media coverage of the Grupo Frontera political controversy revealed significant biases and varying approaches to reporting on the issue.
Mexican media outlets generally took a more critical stance toward Grupo Frontera, often framing the controversy as a betrayal of the Mexican and Latino communities.
These outlets frequently emphasized Grupo Frontera's Mexican roots and the contradiction between their cultural identity and their alleged political sympathies.

Infobae, one of the leading Mexican news outlets, published multiple articles on the controversy, including pieces with headlines such as "Grupo Frontera reacciona a críticas por presunto apoyo a Donald Trump y rechazo a migrantes" (Grupo Frontera reacts to criticism for alleged support for Donald Trump and rejection of migrants).
The coverage often included emotional language and emphasized the negative impact on Grupo Frontera's fanbase, particularly among Mexican fans who felt betrayed.
American media coverage was more varied in its approach.

Some outlets, such as The Direct, provided factual reporting of the controversy without taking a clear stance, focusing on the timeline of events and the various statements from the band and their critics.

Other outlets, such as Latin Times, framed the controversy within the broader context of Latino celebrities and their political responsibilities, noting that while many artists had spoken out against Trump's policies, Grupo Frontera had remained silent for weeks.
The Chicago Sun-Times took a more nuanced approach, suggesting that the connection between Grupo Frontera and Trump might be overblown.
The paper noted that both Grupo Frontera and Trump might simply share a taste in music, rather than political beliefs.
However, this perspective was in the minority, with most media coverage emphasizing the political implications of the controversy.
Social media played a crucial role in amplifying the controversy, with platforms like X and TikTok serving as primary sources of information for many people.
The viral nature of the original video and the subsequent backlash demonstrated the power of social media in shaping public opinion and influencing the trajectory of such controversies.
The Grupo Frontera political controversy meets multiple criteria for notability in the context of Wikipedia standards.
The controversy received extensive coverage in reliable sources, including major news outlets such as EL PAÍS, Infobae, Latin Times, and the Chicago Sun-Times.
The coverage was sustained over several months, from the initial viral video in late January 2025 through the band's responses in February and the ongoing discussions throughout the year.
The controversy also had significant cultural and social impact.

It sparked debates about the role of Latino artists in American society, the expectations placed on cultural figures, and the relationship between personal political beliefs and public responsibility.
The controversy even led to a public feud within the prominent Aguilar family, demonstrating its reach beyond the band itself.
The controversy's impact on Grupo Frontera's career, including lost followers, canceled performances, and damaged reputation, further demonstrates its notability.

The fact that Grupo Frontera was scheduled to perform at major events such as the Sueños Music Festival and faced public protests and petitions for their removal indicates the controversy's significance within the music industry and Latino community.
Additionally, the controversy occurred within a broader context of political tensions in the United States, particularly regarding immigration policies under the Trump administration.
This context gave the controversy added significance, as it represented a microcosm of larger societal divisions.
The Grupo Frontera political controversy has had lasting implications for the band, the Latino music industry, and discussions about political responsibility in entertainment.
For Grupo Frontera specifically, the controversy marked a turning point in their career trajectory.
Prior to the controversy, Grupo Frontera had been experiencing rapid success, winning Latin Grammy awards and collaborating with major artists.

The controversy, however, damaged Grupo Frontera's reputation among a significant portion of their fanbase, particularly in Mexico and among politically active Latino communities in the United States.
The controversy also highlighted broader issues within the Latino music industry regarding political neutrality and public responsibility.
Artists like Ángela Aguilar, who had collaborated with Grupo Frontera on the song "Frágil," faced questions about whether they should sever ties with the band.
The situation created a precedent where artists' political beliefs, or even perceived beliefs, could significantly impact their professional relationships and opportunities.
The controversy also had implications for the broader discussion about Latino identity and political affiliation.
It highlighted the tensions between cultural identity and political ideology, particularly for Mexican-American artists who straddle both cultures.
Grupo Frontera's statement that they are "migrants supporting migrants" while maintaining American citizenship reflected these complex identities.
From a social perspective, the controversy revealed deep divisions within the Latino community regarding political allegiance and the role of public figures.
The intense backlash against Grupo Frontera demonstrated the high expectations placed on Latino artists to represent community values, particularly regarding immigration issues.
The fact that some fans defended Grupo Frontera's right to hold their own political opinions, while others called for their cancellation, showed the complexity of these discussions.
The controversy also had implications for the music industry's approach to artist management and crisis communication.
Grupo Frontera's initial silence and delayed response were widely criticized, suggesting that artists need more sophisticated strategies for handling political controversies.
The speed at which misinformation spread on social media platforms also highlighted the challenges of managing public perception in the digital age.
Looking forward, the Grupo Frontera controversy will likely serve as a case study for other Latino artists navigating political controversies.
It demonstrates the potential consequences of political neutrality in polarized times and the importance of clear, timely communication when addressing sensitive issues.
The controversy also underscores the need for artists to consider the broader implications of their actions and statements, particularly when they have significant influence within their communities.

3.title: Quién es el creador de “No se va”, la versión mexicana de una de las canciones más virales de TikTok
3.description: Uno de los sencillos más escuchados en la plataforma tiene una historia fuera del país, aquí te la contamos.
3.content:
![Image 1: El sencillo de Grupo Frontera](https://www.infobae.com/resizer/v2/OCRHTZMZS5BYXHPDMR7P7RNHK4.jpg?auth=e755328989dd019d607f8a124aeb04e88ee66336c4ad936369a1a863a4d0ccef&smart=true&width=350&height=197&quality=85)

El sencillo de Grupo Frontera es uno de los más escuchados en TikTok Crédito: YT/Grupo Frontera

A dos años de su lanzamiento, la canción _**No se va**_ sigue causando revuelo en redes sociales, pues más allá del rotundo éxito que tuvo, tiene una curiosa historia que inició en España.

La mayoría de las personas identifican el sencillo en las voces de la agrupación mexicana **Grupo Frontera,** quienes se dieron a conocer en 2022 a través de _TikTok_ con el cover de la canción _No se va._

Originarios de Estados Unidos, pero con raíces mexicanas, la banda está conformada por **Adelaido ‘Payo’**(vocalista), **Julián Peña Jr**(percusionista), **Alberto Acosta** (bajo), **Carlos Zamora** (bajo), **Juan Javier Cantú** (acordeón), y **Carlos Guerrero** (batería).

Read more!

![Image 2: Grupo Frontera se dio a](https://www.infobae.com/resizer/v2/6QO54IM52JFJTHHG3O2MTHNEJU.jpg?auth=45293e2d178208c7e64c0a8a42de726832efa3dc37070bdcb16c704fa47e79a5&smart=true&width=350&height=233&quality=85)

Grupo Frontera se dio a conocer con el sencillo 'No se va' (Credito foto: Franco Fafasuli / Infobae)

En sus inicios, la idea de una banda comenzó como un pasatiempo, pero poco a poco fue cambiando, pues decidieron iniciar una aventura en la industria musical. Su debut en YouTube fue con el cover de _Estos celos_ del fallecido **Joan Sebastian**, pero no tuvo gran éxito.

Sin embargo, la historia cambiaría más tarde con el cover _No se va_, el sencillo que los colocó en el centro de la industria y rápidamente se convirtió en uno de los más escuchados en **México, Estados Unidos**y **Colombia.**

Contrario a lo que muchos piensan, la canción _No se va_ la interpretó primero la agrupación colombiana **Morat**, conformada por**Juan Pablo Isaza, Simón Vargas, Juan Pablo Villamil** y**Martín Vargas.**

Dicho sencillo pertenece al disco _Balas perdidas_, el cual fue lanzado en 2018. De acuerdo con la banda colombiana, la idea de crear una canción con más ritmo surgió durante una gira que realizaron por España.

Cuando acudieron a una discoteca se percataron que muchas de sus canciones las ponían ese tipo de lugares, por lo que decidieron crear un tema que fuera específico para las lugares nocturnos, y fue así como nació: **No se va,**escrita por _Juan Pablo Isaza y Juan Pablo Villamil_, integrantes de la banda.

Contrario al cover de Grupo Frontera, la versión original es un tema pop que tiene ritmos bailables pero no logra ser tan contagiosa. Pese a que el sencillo interpretado por Morat fue bien recibido por sus seguidoras, no logró posicionarse como el favorito de la audiencia mexicana.

![Image 3: La agrupación Morat es la](https://www.infobae.com/resizer/v2/MD4LJDZEARCDDNELFGGOWOXKOA.png?auth=373294a9fb601aa6f2544c553bc402d587529cb192f28ca4b22e614f374e5e80&smart=true&width=350&height=180&quality=85)

La agrupación Morat es la creadora del sencillo "No se va" Crédito Morat

De acuerdo con la página de _Billboard_, la agrupación mexicana logró colocar la canción dentro del**listado Hot 100**. Además, se hicieron acreedores de los _Latin American Music Awards_ en la categoría de**Mejor Canción Regional Mexicana del Año.**

Hasta el día de hoy, sigue siendo el sencillo más escuchado de la agrupación, pues ha logrado gran popularidad en diversas plataformas de streaming y ha sido clave en el reconocimiento y éxito de la banda dentro del género norteño.

La pieza destaca por su combinación de melodías pegajosas que resuenan profundamente en la audiencia, que bailó con su propio ritmo y pasos, siendo TikTok, la plataforma que permitió que usuarios de varios países disfrutaran de la canción al ritmo de su elección.

Morat es una **banda colombiana de pop y rock** formada en Bogotá en 2015. La agrupación se ha destacado por sus letras emotivas y su capacidad para fusionar elementos de música folk con el pop latino.

Algunos de sus éxitos más conocidos incluyen: _Cómo te atreves, Amor con hielo, Besos en guerra, Cuando nadie ve, y Yo contigo, tú conmigo._

A lo largo de su trayectoria, han sido acreedores de numerosos premios y han realizado giras internacionales, consolidándose como una de las bandas más influyentes en el panorama musical latinoamericano.

Aunque _No se va_ no es su canción más escuchada; cabe resaltar que el sencillo _**Cómo te atreves**_ se ha convertido en el más escuchado de la agrupación, pues es el que los llevó a la fama internacional.

Grupo Frontera Win Best Norteño Album, Perform Winning Duet at 25th Latin Grammys
=================================================================================

Mexican American Band Shines at the 25th Annual Latin Grammy Awards

![Image 5: Unknown's avatar](https://0.gravatar.com/avatar/6d73a3be5e5586b47b982ac36e0e5dd520041f65710da74ecfeb5342e99bd7d7?s=100&d=https%3A%2F%2F0.gravatar.com%2Favatar%2Fad516503a11cd5ca435acc9bb6523536%3Fs%3D100&r=G)

 by [Tejano Nation Digital](https://tejanonation.net/author/tejan0nation/)

[November 15, 2024](https://tejanonation.net/2024/11/15/grupo-frontera-win-best-norteno-album-perform-winning-duet-at-25th-latin-grammys/)

[Comments 0](https://tejanonation.net/2024/11/15/grupo-frontera-win-best-norteno-album-perform-winning-duet-at-25th-latin-grammys/#respond)

[Embed from Getty Images](http://www.gettyimages.com/detail/2184867360)

**[Grupo Frontera](https://tejanonation.net/tag/grupo-frontera)** has once again made waves in the música Mexicana movement by winning the Latin Grammy Award for Best Norteño Album. The band also delivered a heartfelt performance of their award-winning duet “El Amor De Su Vida” at the 25th annual **[Latin Grammy Awards](https://tejanonation.net/tag/latin-grammy-awards)** in Miami, Florida, on Thursday night.

Advertisement

Fresh off their first U.S. arena tour, Grupo Frontera took the stage at the 2024 Latin Grammy Awards to perform “El Amor De Su Vida,” a track that also won Best Regional Song. Their album “El Comienzo” secured the Best Norteño Album award during the 2024 Latin Grammy Premiere Ceremony.

The band showcased their regional flair with Tejano-style suits and cowboy hats, bringing the essence of life on the US-Mexico border to the Latin Grammy stage. Lead singer **Adelaido “Payo” Solís III** delivered a soulful rendition of “El Amor De Su Vida,” proudly highlighting the group’s roots in Mexico and Texas.

[Follow Tejano Nation on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/tejanonation/)

Advertisement

This performance continued the momentum from their 2023 debut album “El Comienzo,” which featured the genre-bending hit “Un x100to” with **[Bad Bunny](https://tejanonation.net/tag/bad-bunny)** and won the golden gramophone for Best Norteño Album. Grupo Frontera has pushed their cumbia and norteño sound to new heights with their latest album “Jugando a Que No Pasa Nada,” which was nominated for the inaugural Best Contemporary Mexican Music Album category.

“Each member of Grupo Frontera listens and plays different styles, so starting from that, we each had a big say in the genres we wanted to play and styles we wanted to record on this album,” Solís III shared with GRAMMY.com in May.

“Jugando a Que No Pasa Nada” features collaborations with international artists, including **Maluma**, **Nicki Nicole**, **Christian Nodal**, and **Shakira**. Although their collaboration with Shakira, “(Entre Paréntesis),” was nominated for Song Of The Year, it ultimately lost to **Jorge Drexler**.

For a complete list of winners and nominees at the 2024 Latin Grammy Awards, visit the official [Latin Grammy website](https://www.grammy.com/news/2024-latin-grammys-complete-winners-nominees-nominations-list).

Grupo Frontera
--------------

![Image 8: Grupo Frontera](https://www.cmtv.com.ar/imagenes_artistas/3218.webp?Grupo%20Frontera)

Grupo Frontera es una banda estadounidense de Edinburg, Texas, reconocida por su estilo musical que combina elementos de pop latino, cumbia y música norteña. La banda está integrada por Adelaido “Payo” Solís III, Juan Javier Cantú, Julián Peña Jr., Alberto “Beto” Acosta, Carlos Guerrero y Carlos Zamora.

El grupo comienza a grabar en 2019, lanzando versiones de canciones de pop latino y norteño.

Con una trayectoria en constante crecimiento, Grupo Frontera ha cautivado al público con sus interpretaciones y su talento musical.

El 28 de junio de 2023 el grupo estrena el videoclip "[Tulum](https://www.cmtv.com.ar/discos_letras/letra.php?bnid=3201&banda=Peso_Pluma&DS_DS=22958&tmid=181700&tema=TULUM_(FT._GRUPO_FRONTERA))" junto a [Peso Pluma](https://www.cmtv.com.ar/biografia/show.php?bnid=3201&banda=Peso_Pluma).

El 26 de julio la banda se presenta en Argentina en el mítico estadio Luna Park de Buenos Aires.

El 21 de julio lanza una colaboración con [Ke Personajes](https://www.cmtv.com.ar/biografia/show.php?bnid=3156&banda=Ke_Personajes) del single "[Ojitos rojos](https://www.cmtv.com.ar/discos_letras/letra.php?bnid=3156&banda=Ke_Personajes&DS_DS=23105&tmid=182112&tema=OJITOS_ROJOS_(FT._GRUPO_FRONTERA))", este tema se presenta con su videoclip oficial.

El 24 de agosto lanza una colaboración con [Manuel Turizo](https://www.cmtv.com.ar/biografia/show.php?bnid=2504&banda=Manuel_Turizo) llamada “[De lunes a lunes](https://www.cmtv.com.ar/discos_letras/letra.php?bnid=3218&banda=Grupo_Frontera&DS_DS=23331&tmid=183124&tema=DE_LUNES_A_LUNES_(FT._MANUEL_TURIZO))“.

El 25 de agosto presentan el álbum "[El comienzo](https://www.cmtv.com.ar/discos_letras/show.php?bnid=3218&banda=Grupo_Frontera&DS_DS=23332&disco=EL_COMIENZO)" el cual cuenta con grandes colaboraciones.

“Ilegal”: Emiliano Aguilar, hijo de Pepe Aguilar, critica las deportaciones en EE. UU. con su nueva canción. Ante el aumento de deportaciones, el rapero mexicano Emiliano Aguilar presentó "Ilegal", un himno en apoyo a los migrantes mexicanos en EE. UU. Junto al hashtag #TheWallIsNotEnough (El muro no es suficiente), el rapero Emiliano Aguilar presentó su nuevo sencillo "Ilegal", una fuerte crítica a las deportaciones en Estados Unidos tras la llegada al poder del presidente Donald Trump. "Todos somos habitantes del mundo y en nuestra tierra nadie debería ser ilegal", afirma Aguilar en el videoclip de la canción, la cual había anunciado en sus redes sociales como un himno para los migrantes trabajadores que enfrentan el asedio de las autoridades estadounidenses. En un video promocional en TikTok, el artista expresó su enojo ante la situación migratoria y cómo el gobierno de Trump busca expulsar a quienes trabajan por un mejor futuro. "Hice esta canción específicamente para esas personas. No tiene nada que ver con la calle, sino con los trabajadores que no merecen ser perseguidos solo por intentar ganarse la vida en ese país", declaró Emiliano Aguilar. Protesta contra las deportaciones. Junto al rapero Turek Hem, Aguilar convierte "Ilegal" en una protesta musical contra la deportación de migrantes, quienes contribuyen al desarrollo económico de EE. UU. "Aunque el muro esté más alto, no nos va a parar. Encontraremos la manera de cruzar", dice el coro de la canción, que denuncia la crisis migratoria y las políticas restrictivas del gobierno estadounidense. Durante el rap, los artistas también critican la falta de apoyo del gobierno mexicano a los migrantes y las medidas adoptadas por Trump. Migrantes buscan trabajo, no delinquir. La crítica de Emiliano Aguilar y Turek Hem no se limitó a la canción "Ilegal". En una entrevista con EFE, ambos destacaron que los migrantes mexicanos llegan a Estados Unidos con el propósito de trabajar y construir un futuro mejor, algo que muchas veces no es posible en sus países de origen. "Son mexicanos que cruzan para allá para trabajar, no todos van a delinquir. Es una tontearía pensar que todos los mexicanos son así, porque nuestra gente sí trabaja. De hecho, trabajan mucho más que muchos en Estados Unidos, la neta", comentó Aguilar. Mexicanos: símbolo de esfuerzo y trabajo. En la entrevista, Aguilar criticó las acciones del presidente Donald Trump y resaltó la dedicación de los migrantes:. "Los mexicanos son gente trabajadora que se gana la vida honestamente. Ahora están construyendo un muro más alto, y eso no es digno. Hice esta canción porque estoy muy enojado y quería expresar todo esto". Junto al hashtag _#TheWallIsNotEnough_ (El muro no es suficiente), el rapero **Emiliano Aguilar presentó su nuevo sencillo _"Ilegal"_, una fuerte crítica a las deportaciones en Estados Unidos** tras la llegada al poder del presidente Donald Trump.

"**Todos somos habitantes del mundo y en nuestra tierra nadie debería ser ilegal**", afirma Aguilar en el videoclip de la canción, la cual había anunciado en sus redes sociales como un himno para los migrantes trabajadores que enfrentan el asedio de las autoridades estadounidenses.

En un video promocional en TikTok, el artista expresó **su enojo ante la situación migratoria y cómo el gobierno de Trump busca expulsar a quienes trabajan por un mejor futuro.**

"Hice esta canción específicamente para esas personas. No tiene nada que ver con la calle, sino con los trabajadores que**no merecen ser perseguidos solo por intentar ganarse la vida en ese país**", declaró Emiliano Aguilar.

Protesta contra las deportaciones
---------------------------------

Junto al rapero Turek Hem, Aguilar convierte _"Ilegal"_ en una protesta musical contra la deportación de migrantes, quienes contribuyen al desarrollo económico de EE. UU.

"Aunque el muro esté más alto, no nos va a parar. Encontraremos la manera de cruzar", dice el coro de la canción, que denuncia la crisis migratoria y las políticas restrictivas del gobierno estadounidense.

Durante el rap, **los artistas también critican la falta de apoyo del gobierno mexicano a los migrantes y las medidas adoptadas por Trump**.

Migrantes buscan trabajo, no delinquir
--------------------------------------

La crítica de Emiliano Aguilar y Turek Hem no se limitó a la canción _"Ilegal"_. En una entrevista con EFE, ambos destacaron que los migrantes mexicanos llegan a Estados Unidos con el propósito de trabajar y construir un futuro mejor, algo que muchas veces no es posible en sus países de origen.

En una entrevista con EFE, ambos destacaron que los migrantes mexicanos llegan a Estados Unidos con el propósito de trabajar y construir un futuro mejor, algo que muchas veces no es posible en sus países de origen. "Son mexicanos que cruzan para allá para trabajar, no todos van a delinquir. Es una tontearía pensar que todos los mexicanos son así, porque nuestra gente sí trabaja. De hecho, trabajan mucho más que muchos en Estados Unidos, la neta", comentó Aguilar. Mexicanos: símbolo de esfuerzo y trabajo. En la entrevista, Aguilar criticó las acciones del presidente Donald Trump y resaltó la dedicación de los migrantes:. "Los mexicanos son gente trabajadora que se gana la vida honestamente. Ahora están construyendo un muro más alto, y eso no es digno. Hice esta canción porque estoy muy enojado y quería expresar todo esto". El rapero explicó que "Ilegal" denuncia las deportaciones masivas de Trump y envía un mensaje de solidaridad a quienes viven con miedo en EE. UU. "Ojalá que esta rola llegue a sus oídos y a los del gobierno, que se escuche alto y se convierta en un himno para toda esta gente que está siendo expulsada de sus hogares", agregó. Un mensaje de apoyo desde la frontera. El rapero Turek Hem, quien también participa en la canción, compartió con EFE que el videoclip de "Ilegal" fue grabado en el muro fronterizo, un símbolo de la lucha migrante. "Todo esto es una gran injusticia, lo que está pasando con nuestra gente. Esta canción es para ellos, para ofrecerles nuestro apoyo incondicional", afirmó. "Quiero que este mensaje se escuche por todos lados, que todos se sientan identificados y unidos", agregó Hem. "No pierdan la fe". Aguilar expresó su tristeza por la difícil situación que viven los migrantes:. "Me da mucha tristeza ver a tantas familias expulsadas de EE. UU. como si fueran animales. Si con mi música puedo generar un pequeño cambio, lo haré". "Quiero decirles que no pierdan la fe. Sé que están pasando por tiempos difíciles, pero los mexicanos nos importan. Estamos con ustedes", concluyó Aguilar.

5.title: Grupo Frontera y Peso Pluma hacen historia para México dentro del Billboard Hot 100
5.description: Entre ambos actos mexicanos, ostentan 12 lugares en la prestigiosa lista
5.content:
![Image 1: Peso Pluma y Grupo Frontera](https://www.infobae.com/resizer/v2/TPYTCFM5LZEJBBEZJUUZNVJUKA.jpg?auth=4327de024b73969a90ba71963b1d17bc547f683c38016ed65f270b26f5159dcc&smart=true&width=350&height=197&quality=85)

Peso Pluma y Grupo Frontera han hecho historia con 12 canciones posicionadas en el Billboard Hot 100. Foto: Instagram/@pesopluma, Billboard, Instagram/@payo_frontera

México continúa destacándose en la industria de la música gracias al regional mexicano y su subgénero que hoy está dando mucho de qué hablar: los corridos tumbados.

En ambos casos, los números han sido meramente históricos, pues tanto **Peso Pluma** como **Grupo Frontera** se han encargado de llevar el género a los primeros lugares del **Billboard Hot 100**, lista que recopila los 100 sencillos más vendidos en Estados Unidos. Estos artistas no sólo están en los primeros lugares, sino que además, cuentan con un total de 12 temas que inundan el**Billboard Hot 100**, un récord histórico no sólo para el género, sino para la música mexicana.

Primero está el caso de **Grupo Frontera**, agrupación que ya había tenido un gran recibimiento por su interpretación del tema _No se va,_ original de la banda **Morat.** Sin embargo, su más reciente colaborción con Bad Bunny titulada _Unx100To_ les ha dado un éxito sin precedentes en su carrera.

Read more!

En entrevista con _RollingStone México_, el vocalista de **Grupo Frontera**, **Adelaido “Payo” Solís III**, habló sobre la experencia tan única que fue grabar su tema más exitoso con el que es hoy en día el exponente de reggaeton más importante del mundo.

![Image 2: La colaboración de Grupo Frontera](https://www.infobae.com/resizer/v2/TUZZST75WRAOHDQQDPTRPXSCKE.jpg?auth=2117a213186de9f657757207125e1d8d356a46ff5ff17bb5c3772b9769d392b1&smart=true&width=350&height=197&quality=85)

La colaboración de Grupo Frontera con Bad Bunny se convirtió en la más exitosa de su carrera. Hoy en día se encuentra en el número 15 del Billboard Hot 100. (Foto: Instagram/@grupofrontera)

“Grabamos la canción y en el video también le dimos una pasada a la grabación de nosotros y luego llega **Edgar Barrera**, que es el compositor, y dijo le vamos a poner un cambio, vamos a cambiar la canción. Nos quedamos como _¿Pero cómo? ¿Qué va a pasar?_ Nosotros no estábamos preparados. Y dijo: “Confía en mí, confía en mí. Todo va a estar bien. Es por lo bueno”. Y luego llega Benito caminando en cámara lenta hacia nosotros y nos quedamos como con cara de enamorados. Y así básicamente surgió el tema”.

Hasta el momento, Grupo Frontera cuenta con cuatro temas en el Billboard Hot 100:

*   Puesto 15: _Unx100to_ con Bad Bunny
*   Puesto 52: _Bebe Dame_ conFuerza Regida
*   Puesto 82: _Que vuelvas_ con Carin León
*   Puesto 99: _Di que sí_ con Grupo Marca Registrada

Lo de **Peso Pluma** también ha sido una historia por demás extraordinaria. Con tan sólo tres años dentro de la industria musical, **Hassan Emilio Kabande Laija** (verdadero nombre de **Peso Pluma**, se ha consagrado como el primer músico de regional mexicano que se presenta en el legendario show de Jimmy Fallon para interpretar su más grande éxito: _Ella Baila Sola_, canción en compañía de Eslabón Armado y que hoy ostenta el quinto lugar del _Billboard Hot 100_.

En una entrevista para la misma _Billboard_, las mentes maestras detrás de esta canción compartieron la anécdota de cómo surgió. **Pedro Tovar**, vocalista de **Eslabón Armado**, aseguró que él fue quien escribió la canción a petición de “**Doble P**”, además de cantársela por teléfono para conocer su reacción de inmediato.

![Image 3:  "Ella baila sola" de](https://www.infobae.com/resizer/v2/MC6MDEHK75D2ZEQP6LVANFAV2Y.jpg?auth=6ca4f22388317ab0738f8ee4a17d1507b90d3d78d8f7125d9b93aaf4848ba732&smart=true&width=350&height=197&quality=85)

 "Ella baila sola" de Peso Pluma y Eslabón Armado tuvo tanto éxito que fue presentada en vivo en el show de Jimmy Fallon. (@MTVLA)

“Peso me pidió que le enviara canciones, así que escribí ‘Ella baila sola’ después de que intercambiamos mensajes. Lo llamé justo después de que terminé de escribirla. Recuerdo que estaba en un aeropuerto y le dije, ‘Hola bro, tengo la canción’. Me pidió que se la enviara, pero decidí cantársela. ‘Para poder ver tu reacción’, le expliqué. Fue amor a primera vista. Estaba muy emocionado”.

Por su parte, **Hassan** comentó que se trata de una canción con la que cualquiera podría identificarse, razón por la que la gente la recibió tan bien.

“Es una canción con la que la mayoría del público se puede relacionar, aparte de tener los elementos de los instrumentos que la hacen diferente. La verdad la gente la recibió y la disfruta tanto como nosotros”.

Al igual que **Grupo Frontera, Peso Pluma** no sólo ha colocado _**Ella Baila Sola**_ en Billboard Hot 100. Son un total de ocho piezas las que el originario de Zapopan, Jalisco, tiene coladas en esta prestigiosa lista.

Estas son las canciones que **Peso Pluma** mantiene al día de hoy en el Billboard Hot 100:

*   Puesto 5: _Ella baila sola_ con Eslabón Armado
*   Puesto 12: _La bebé_ con Yng Lvcas
*   Puesto 32: _Por la noches_
*   Puesto 35: _PRC_ con Natanael Cano
*   Puesto 40: _AMG_ con Natanael Cano y Gabito Ballesteros
*   Puesto 59: _El Azul_ con Junior H
*   Puesto 88: _Chanel_ con Becky G
*   Puesto 90: _Igualito a mi apa_ con Fuerza Regida

Hasta el momento, estos los primeros 10 lugares de Billboard Top 100. Foto: Billboard

GRUPO FONTERA
-------------

Por medio de un video, la agrupación reveló su verdadera postura sobre el presidente americano
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Wendy Guevara reacciona a la política de Donald Trump que solo reconoce dos géneros: hombre y mujer](https://www.mundodeportivo.com/us/estrellas-latinas/20250216/715900/wendy-guevara-reacciona-politica-donald-trump-reconoce-dos-generos-hombre-mujer.html "Wendy Guevara reacciona a la política de Donald Trump que solo reconoce dos géneros: hombre y mujer")
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 5: Grupo Frontera niega apoyo a Donald Trump: “Nosotros somos migrantes”](https://www.mundodeportivo.com/us/files/image_449_220/files/fp/uploads/2025/02/24/67bca6b00ebfb.r_d.540-360-4157.jpeg)

Grupo Frontera niega apoyo a Donald Trump: “Nosotros somos migrantes”

Instagram @grupofrontera

*   [Daniela Machorro](https://www.mundodeportivo.com/us/autor/daniela-machorro.html)  

Actualizado a 24/02/2025 13:22 EST

**Grupo Frontera** aprovechó su cuenta oficial de Instagram para **negar**el **apoyo**a**[Donald Trump](https://www.mundodeportivo.com/us/estrellas-latinas/20250216/715900/wendy-guevara-reacciona-politica-donald-trump-reconoce-dos-generos-hombre-mujer.html "Wendy Guevara reacciona a la política de Donald Trump que solo reconoce dos géneros: hombre y mujer")**, luego de especulaciones en torno a que la agrupación de regional mexicano estaba a favor de la **política migratoria** del presidente de Estados Unidos.

Lee también
[Belinda y Ángela Aguilar: así fue su polémico encuentro en Premio Lo Nuestro](https://www.mundodeportivo.com/us/estrellas-latinas/20250221/716381/belinda-angela-aguilar-asi-polemico-encuentro-premio-nuestro.html)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Daniel Ballesteros![Image 6: Belinda y Ángela Aguilar: así fue su encuentro en Premio Lo Nuestro](https://www.mundodeportivo.com/us/files/image_104_108/uploads/2025/02/21/67b81276b9dae.jpeg)
Por medio de un video, la agrupación integrada por Adelaido “Payo” Solís III, Juan Javier Cantú, Julián Peña Jr., Alberto “Beto” Acosta, Carlos Guerrero y Brian Ortega, reveló su **verdadera postura** sobre el presidente americano.

“**Nosotros somos migrantes**, nuestros papás son migrantes y así, derechito se lo decimos, nosotros **no apoyamos a ningún partido político que esté en contra de los migrantes**”, dijo contundente "Payo", líder de la famosa agrupación.

“**En Tik Tok han salido tantas noticias falsas**, que estar saliendo a desmentir cada cosa... no acabamos... Las únicas opiniones que valen dentro de Grupo Frontera son las de los integrantes, los demás no pueden hablar por nosotros”, agregó el músico.

“**Somos migrantes, estamos para los [migrantes](https://www.mundodeportivo.com/us/actualidad/20250214/715769/redadas-ice-escuelas-denver-frenarlas.html "Redadas de ICE en escuelas: ¿Puede Denver frenarlas?")**... y a los fans, ustedes saben lo que hemos hecho, ustedes saben lo que hemos apoyado a nuestra raza, ya sea en México, en Estados Unidos o en dónde estemos y eso es lo que representa Grupo Frontera”, finalizó.

> [](https://www.instagram.com/p/DGZDXqOPY20/)

Lee también
[Paquita la del Barrio y sus 5 canciones más escuchadas en Spotify](https://www.mundodeportivo.com/us/estrellas-latinas/20250217/715965/paquita-barrio-5-canciones-mas-escuchadas-spotify.html)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Daniela Machorro![Image 7: Paquita la del Barrio](https://www.mundodeportivo.com/us/files/image_104_108/files/fp/uploads/2025/02/17/67b38aef57487.r_d.577-360-1669.png)
Grupo Frontera es vinculado con Donald Trump

​
-----------------------------------------------

Recordemos que el mes pasado, **Grupo Frontera fue vinculado con Donald Trump** por la tiktoker **Sarah Jasmine**, quien aseguró que los músicos habían expresado abiertamente su simpatía por el actual mandatario estadounidense.

“**Hay un video donde se ve a Grupo Frontera diciendo que votan por Trump**. Ahora que se está cancelando a diferentes influencers latinos que apoyan a Donald, debo hablar de esto porque los vi”, declaró la joven.

La joven creadora de contenido, aseguró que las evidencias ya habían sido borradas de los diferentes perfiles de los integrantes; sin embargo, un**nuevo video**, esta vez por parte de uno de los familiares, volvió a poner en duda a los intérpretes de 'Que vuelvas', 'No se va' y 'un x100to', entre otros éxitos.

En las imágenes aparecía la abuelita de "Payo", vocalista del grupo, ‘bailando la canción 'YMCA', de Village People, misma agrupación que cantó durante el cierre de campaña del entonces **candidato republicano**.
